query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of a reactive dopant (e.g., aluminum) into the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of an adaptive oxide nanocomposite layer during sliding, thereby lowering both friction and wear rates across a wide temperature range (RT to 800 °C) compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy exhibiting typical friction and wear behavior without self-adaptive lubrication.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a minor fraction (e.g., approximately 3–5 wt%) of a reactive element such as aluminum into the CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tests conducted under consistent load in ambient, oxidative environments spanning room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The reactive dopant is expected to generate an ultra-fine, adaptive oxide nanocomposite layer (rich in aluminum oxide) on the sliding interface during wear.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the aluminum reacts with oxygen to form a continuous, finely grained oxide layer that acts as a deformable, protective glaze. This adaptive layer distributes frictional stress, minimizes adhesive interactions, and reduces oxidative wear, thereby maintaining low friction coefficients and wear rates over a broad temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-doped CoCrFeNi alloy is predicted to exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates across the full temperature range compared to the undoped baseline, with the oxide nanolayer playing a key role at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: The undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, which lacks an adaptive surface layer, shows higher friction and wear, especially under high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under moderate loads with an ambient oxidative environment; extreme conditions (e.g., highly reducing atmospheres or very high loads) might suppress the formation or effectiveness of the oxide nanolayer.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dopant concentration, the kinetics of oxide layer formation during dynamic sliding, and the performance under varying loads require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one set doped with 3–5 wt% aluminum. Conduct controlled dry sliding wear tests over the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under identical loads in an ambient oxidizing atmosphere. Characterize the surfaces post-testing using microscopy and spectroscopy to assess the formation and quality of any oxide nanocomposite layer, and quantify friction coefficients and wear rates.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature
Surface layer thickness, composition, and microstructure (via electron microscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear across the tested temperature range, or if no consistent oxide nanocomposite layer forms relative to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Reactive wear protection through strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces

Abstract: Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude. The reactive wear protection strategy offers a pathway for designing ultra-wear resistant alloys
